title: The Revival, the secrets of prayer
hookLine: presence of heart, understanding, reverence, awe, hope, shame
tomorrow: skipping lunch is easy. so what's the hard part of a fast?

lines: YOUR BODY BOWS, YOUR HEAD WANDERS.
cards: You're halfway through, and you realize your mind left a while ago. Your body has been bowing; your head has been rewriting an email. It can happen in prayer, or in any ritual repeated often.
Al-Bukhari keeps a scene that starts right there. A man walks into the mosque, prays, then comes over and greets the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
The Prophet returns the greeting and says: go back and pray, for you have not prayed. The man prays again. Comes back.
Same answer. Again. Finally he says: by the One who sent you, I can't do any better.

teach.b: The Prophet teaches him slowly: stand, recite, bow until you're at rest in the bowing, rise until you're upright, prostrate until you're at rest.
The missing piece was stillness. He had done every movement and rushed through all of them. Al-Ghazali takes that further in the Revival, in a book on the secrets of prayer.
A body at rest is the outside.
He asks about the inside, and names six inner things that give prayer its life. Presence of heart: being there, not elsewhere. Understanding: knowing what the words mean as you say them.
Reverence: honoring the One you're speaking to. Awe: the fear that comes from glimpsing his greatness. Hope: expecting his mercy.
And shame: an honest sense of your own shortfall. He's careful about one thing.

A jurist judges whether a prayer is valid by its outside, and a distracted prayer may still be valid. But al-Ghazali asks a different question: how much of it reached God? That's the surprise of the story.
The man's prayer looked like a prayer. Rushed and absent, it wasn't yet one, and the Prophet kept sending him back until stillness made room for the heart.

how: Muslims pray the daily prayers, aiming for stillness in each position; teachers who follow al-Ghazali encourage presence of heart and understanding of the Arabic words being recited.

games.q: your friend says she prays so fast she's done before she's even started. she asks where to begin. what fits today's story?
o: slow the body first: at rest in each position, so the heart has room.
add more prayers each day until it starts to feel real.
stop praying until the feeling comes back on its own.
games.why: the Prophet's teaching to the man who rushed began with the body: at rest in each position. al-Ghazali's inner six build on that stillness.

practice: Choose one of the six: presence, understanding, reverence, awe, hope, or shame. Close your eyes and let that single word set the tone of the sit. If you pray later today, carry the same word into one prayer.

wordCard.voice: The Revival, again: in its book on prayer, al-Ghazali names six inner things, from presence of heart to shame, that bring a prayer to life.

orig.note: Arabic: hudur al-qalb, presence of heart, the first of al-Ghazali's six inner things in prayer.
